en: The Seventieth Chapter of the *Śāstra-saṃgraha* Compiled by Shi Dunlun:
The Third Section on the Victorious Merits of the Radiance of Wisdom. First, it is explained that the light of wisdom possesses five victorious merits.
Furthermore, it is distinguished that the light of wisdom possesses fifteen virtues.
Regarding the statement in the preceding section that it "bestows the foremost bliss" and "leads to the foremost destination," Xuánzàng says:
Enlightenment is called the supreme bliss;
Nirvana is called the supreme destination.
Now, this is explained.
Having attained the bliss of the Dharma in the present, one subsequently proceeds toward Bodhi and Nirvana.
The following section distinguishes the excellence of the wisdom-virtue from that of external [objects].
Regarding the statement in the middle that "darkness exists" as being contradictory, it refers to the time when external light arises.
Furthermore, while there is a mutual contradiction between subtle darkness and its opposite,
when the light of wisdom arises, there is no such contradiction with ignorance and darkness; thus,
[ignorance] cannot conceal what has already been revealed by [wisdom], nor can it conceal that which is capable of being revealed by [wisdom].
There are two explanations for this.
The first explanation states:
external light cannot conceal that which it has itself revealed.
Just as when fire has already illuminated an object that has been revealed,
even though sunlight is superior, it cannot obscure it so that the illuminated object does not appear;
the light of wisdom is not like that.
When superior wisdom conceals the teachings already revealed by inferior wisdom,
those teachings then become obscure and fail to arise.
A second explanation states:

The phenomena already revealed and made manifest by conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna) are, when observed by ultimate knowledge (tattva-jñāna), seen as having their conventional characteristics obscured; thus, what was previously revealed is now termed "hidden.
External light is not like this.
Regarding the statement that "contradiction harms vision, whereas non-contradiction does not harm vision":
just as the light of the sun contradicts and harms visual perception,
the light of wisdom only increases insight and enhances visual perception.
The fourth [section] clarifies six sets of three dharmas.
Regarding the three that bring about discipline and excellence:
the first is the elimination of unwholesome karma.
Second, the suppression of the fetters;
third, the eradication of the seeds and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
These are the three types of brahmins.
First, those who are progressing toward the state of a brahmin are the four candidates for the fruits.
Second, those who abide in the fruits are the three fruits of training (*śaikṣa*).
Third, those who have reached the ultimate are the fruit of no-more-training (*aśaikṣa*).
"Brahman" (梵) is a term from the Western [Indic] lands; its translation here is "quiescence" (寂靜), which refers to *nirvāṇa*.
"Vow" (志) is a term from this region [of China].
Because they seek the state of Brahmā, they are called *brahmacārin* (Brahma-farers).
As for the term *śramaṇa*, it is translated as "diligent laborer" (*qínláo*).
Just as in the path of non-obstruction (*anantarya-mārga*), one exerts diligent effort and comprehensive power to sever all afflictions; therefore, they are called "diligent laborers."
It is also called "stopping evil.
First, regarding those who are merely nominally brahmins:
this refers to those such as the barbarians north of the Snowy Mountains who claim for themselves the title of brahmin.
Second, the brahmins of lineage refers to those of the highest caste among the four castes within the five regions of India.
Third, the brahmins of correct practice.
This refers to those of the four castes who have left the household life to cultivate mundane and supramundane right practices.
"Brāhmaṇa" is translated here as "Pure Resolve.
Fifth, the section clarifies the destruction of the equipment of *śīla* (ethical discipline).
First, it is explained that ethical discipline (*śīla*) is destroyed by four conditions:
first, one who commits an offense regarding a transgression without remainder (*anavaśeṣa-āpatti*) violates the first aggregate;
second, one who does not repent regarding a transgression with remainder (*sāvaśeṣa-āpatti*) violates the latter four aggregates.
The latter two [purities] may be understood.

Next, the perfection [of these purities] is explained. Regarding the statement, "the purity of the associates refers to the purity of view, conduct, and livelihood": it means that the purity of the associates consists in the purity of one's views, conduct, and livelihood.
This is obtained through the preceding preparatory application;
alternatively, the causes and conditions are termed "auxiliaries.
When one receives the precepts with a mind of right view, it is called "purity of view."
Physical and verbal conduct free from wrong views is called purity of deportment (*īryāpatha-śuddhi*).
Seeking the reception of the precepts solely for the sake of *nirvāṇa* is called purity of livelihood (*ājīva-śuddhi*).

As for natural purity (*svabhāva-śuddhi*), it refers to respectfully training in accordance with the teachings; one who trains in all its parts is one who upholds the precepts and thereby purifies them.
To revere and hold the *prātimokṣa* in high esteem is called "respectful emulation" (*satkṛtyānuśikṣaṇā*),
as it is equivalent to the Buddha remaining in the world.
Because one attains [the benefits] in full— whether the precepts received are many or few— it is called "complete emulation" (*sakalānuśikṣaṇā*).
Regarding the statement "five kinds of places where one should not go," these refer to the houses of butchers, prostitutes, and so forth.
The sixth [point] clarifies the thorough protection of the sense faculties and the recognition of their faults.
This can be understood according to the text.
The seventh [point] clarifies the elimination of eight factors through moderation in eating.
Regarding the phrase "the life-faculty perishes":
If one eats excessively, the life-faculty will be destroyed;
those who are weak from hunger are like the non-Buddhist outsiders who abstain from food.
By knowing the proper measure of food, one is able to eliminate and sever [such suffering].
The eighth clarifies the yoga of awakening.
One who awakens while wasting [the opportunity] does so because they give rise to defiled cognitions.
One who sleeps while wasting [the opportunity] refers to one who again falls asleep at that time, taking a defiled mind as the condition.
The ninth section clarifies the six types of renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*).
Only the first two and the last four need to be explained, as the others are easily understood.
Regarding the phrase "not conforming to a single destination," this refers to the bodies and so forth of the miserable realms (*durgati*).
Second, non-conformity regarding birth refers to birth from eggs or moisture and so forth.
Third, non-conformity regarding diligence refers to being prone to indolence.
Fourth, non-conformity regarding obstacles refers to being beset by many hindrances and difficulties.
The five types of non-conformity with delight refer to being stained by delight and so forth.
Regarding the terms "instruction" and "realization": instruction refers to the *āgama* (scriptural tradition), while realization refers to realized wisdom (*adhigama-jñāna*).
These two [types of] implicit formulations are thus implicitly established.
The tenth [section] clarifies how the desire for wholesome dharmas arises through four powers,
as stated in the text.
Eleventh, the perfection of renunciation (*pravrajyā-saṃpad*).
Within this, "perfection of dwelling" refers to staying in places such as cemeteries or at the foot of trees.
Twelfth, the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃpad*).
This is precisely the incomplete renunciation present before one.
Thirteen: explaining the two powers and the four faculties of restraint.
Regarding the power of discernment and the power of cultivation:

The wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) is the power of analytical discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāna-bala*); the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) is the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā-bala*).
Regarding the four kinds of protection, Jing said:
Guarding the objective sphere means protecting oneself against external objects so that the mind does not become distracted.
Guarding against afflictions means not giving rise to craving or distress regarding those very same objects.
Here, "afflictions" is used as a general term.
The outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) and the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), as well as their active manifestations and seeds, are protected against in two ways.
When afflictions do not arise, this is called "protecting against the outbursts.
Because the outbursts do not arise, they do not perfume [the mind] to form seeds; this is called "protecting against the latent tendencies."
It may also be protected from afflictions;
that is, when one practices while remaining in a state of meditative equipoise, one is free from attachment, sorrow, and so forth regarding objects.
This refers to the time when one initiates application during the stage of formal meditative absorption (*samāhita*).
Being free from desire, grief, and so forth, one guards the faculty of the eye;

this is called guarding against the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*). To realize the guarding of the faculties is to guard against the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), because in the state of a distracted mind, the outbursts of the eye faculty do not arise due to such guarding.
This is because the seeds of delusion are prevented from arising due to the absence of their conditions;
only then can it be proven that the protection of the eye faculty is [the function] of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*). Tai says:
Regarding the phrase "those whose conduct is equal," this means that the afflictions of a person with equal parts (*sabhāga*) can be guarded against; however,
those who are predominant (*adhimātra*) cannot be guarded against.
Those with few afflictions do not need to guard [the mind].
Now, this is explained:
it refers to when a practitioner at the stage of "equality" (samatā) is associated with a wholesome or neutral state of being.
The state of guarding through mindfulness is called the "state of equanimity.
Fourteenth, it clarifies the perfection of moderation in eating;
herein, the first [of the four types of antidotes] is the antidote of reliance, because it relies upon correct discernment.
Second, "distancing from what is to be countered" means not engaging in dissipation, arrogance, negligence, and so forth.
Third, "relying on white actions" means causing the body to abide in peace.
Fourth, "relying on the basis" means practicing the path for the sake of temporary support.
Regarding "the fivefold discrimination," this refers to the discrimination between what is sinful and what is non-sinful,
and so forth. As for the various phrases following this,
Master Jing relates the words of the Tripiṭaka Master:
Because the sensation of retribution is experienced as hunger and thirst, it is called "old sensation," which arises from hunger.
Apart from the sensation of retribution, the category of "remedial sensation" (pratipakṣa-vedanā) applies to all three moral natures;
for whenever food is obtained, there is the experience of feeling its utility.
Regarding painful feelings arising from nutriment: apart from those feelings that are retribution,
all other categories of feeling pertain to all three moral natures (wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral),
because at the time one obtains nutriment, there is the experience of feeling its painful aspect.
Regarding the statement that "painful sensations arise from food," the following passage beginning with "nurturing" explains the scriptural text.
As for the statement that one should sit during the first, second, and fourth hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*):
This means that greed, hatred, restlessness, and remorse are to be countered during seated meditation;
among the third set of hindrances, the hindrance of sleepiness is to be countered during walking meditation;
and among the fifth set of hindrances, [the remaining ones] are to be countered at all times.
Regarding the single hindrance of doubt, one may employ deliberation during both the periods of walking and sitting as its antidote;
this is for the purpose of abandoning the lion-like, long-lasting, and extremely heavy loss of mindfulness that leads to uninterrupted sleep.
Because the lion, being fearless, sleeps much day and night, it is said that he is "free from" them. Tai says:
"Before eating, the bodily sensation arises due to the contact of hunger."
What is called "the feeling of having previously experienced [hunger]" arises from the contact of hunger.
The arising of painful feeling due to eating in excess is caused by food itself.
Eating in moderation to sustain one's life serves to increase the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
The power of its sustenance is that it can counteract the afflictions to be subdued, such as the sensations arising from hunger.
Eating in moderation is dwelling in happiness in the present life.
Because there is no unwholesome conduct after having eaten, this is the purification of the field of merit through giving.
When about to sleep, one should first contemplate the intention to rise early during the latter part of the night.
Fifteenth is dwelling with clear comprehension.
The middle statement, "for the purpose of making the two bases pliant," refers to this.
First, one dispels drowsiness by means of the body that served as the basis for the preceding experience;
second, one dispels fatigue by means of the body that served as the basis for the prior cultivation of teachings and the analytical determination of their meaning.
One also skillfully knows the proper measure.
Furthermore, sleep and fatigue serve as the two bases for the body.
The sixteen clarities subsume the eight formative forces of abandonment (*aṣṭau prahāṇasaṃskārāḥ*) within the four limbs.
Regarding the statement, "By means of right mindfulness, one guards against the secondary afflictions that have not yet arisen in relation to calm abiding (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā)":
concentration is termed calm abiding and wisdom is termed insight;
laxity and excitement, which obstruct concentration and wisdom, are termed the secondary afflictions of calm abiding and insight.
Seventeenth, it clarifies that the four dharmas serve as the predominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the meditative concentration attained;
this may be understood according to the text.
Eighteenth, it clarifies the seven dharmas.
Those who wish to realize samādhi should correctly understand this.
Jing says: First, the cause for retrogression from internal concentration is laziness.
Because mental indolence gives rise to lethargy and drowsiness,
indolence is the cause [of the first].
Second, regarding the external cause for the decline of meditative concentration, it is called restlessness.
Due to external objects, agitation serves as the cause for distraction toward the five sensory desires;
internally, one falls away from meditative concentration through lethargy and sleep.
The arising of lethargy and so forth from indolence is precisely what constitutes decline.
This refers either to the decline of what has not yet been attained or the decline of what has already been attained.
When internal conditions act as obstacles, it is termed "internal."
The "reversal of the four external concentrations" refers to those who are distracted by the five types of sensual desire.
Because they grasp at the five desires through external agitation, this also pertains to both types of reversal.
It is called "external" because external conditions act as obstacles.
Regarding the five internal meditative absorptions, their decline, their causes, and their remedies: one who correctly observes by properly grasping the signs is able to abandon laziness,
lethargy, and sleep through the proper apprehension of the characteristics of the object.
Regarding the sixth, the external concentration on decline and its antidote: this refers to observing the impurity of the body.
By contemplating one's own body and the bodies of others as impure, one is able to eliminate restlessness and the five sensual desires.
Seventh, regarding the support for the antidotes to those two, namely the perception of light (*ālokasaṃjñā*):
the initial observation of the objective aspect and the meditation on impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*) both rely upon the perception of light.
T'ai states:
The first two secondary afflictions arise by taking either the internal or the external as their object, serving as the causes for the regression of meditative concentration.
The next two secondary afflictions likewise take both the internal and external as their objects, constituting the very essence of the regression of concentration.

The fifth [secondary affliction] correctly grasps the three specific antidotes—calm abiding (*śamatha*), exertion (*pragraha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*)—which counteract the first and second [regressions].
The sixth, the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), serves as the antidote to the second and fourth [hindrances].
This is because the second and fourth arise from external objects of the five desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*), giving rise to excitation (*auddhatya*) and distraction (*vikṣepa*);
therefore, the contemplation of impurity acts as their remedy.
The seventh [stage], the perception of light (*āloka-saṃjñā*), serves as the means (*upāya*) by which the fifth and sixth antidotes can arise;
therefore, it acts as the support (*āśraya*) for those two antidotes.
Both explanations are largely identical.
Nineteenth, the nine phrases concerning the cultivation of the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness as explained in the sutra.
Regarding the phrase "in the body," it means to dwell well in mindfulness regarding this body; regarding the phrase "in the body of suchness," it means...
Contemplating the suchness of the body is called "abiding well in mindfulness.
Alternatively, it refers to supramundane wisdom alone;
that is to say, for one who practices the path of internal śamatha.
When wisdom is concentrated on a tranquil object, that is precisely *śamatha*;
or, it refers to those who possess exclusively supramundane vision,
namely those who proceed by way of *vipaśyanā*.
Because one must investigate what is seen, this is designated as the path of *vipaśyanā*.
Regarding the twenty types of persons established based on the aforementioned generosity,
these five types are explained in accordance with worldly convention.
They are collectively termed "superior practice" (*adhiśīla*), because five types of persons are established based upon this superior practice.
Thus it is said: "Based on the superior, five kinds [of persons] are established," and so forth.
If one relies on the principle, the second and fifth are noble and thus designated as "superior";
the first is mundane;
and the third and fourth belong to the non-Buddhists.
One whose conduct is inverted cannot be called superior.
The first person has three [characteristics]:
namely, they delight in birth in the desire realm and take pleasure in the desires of the desire realm.
This is one interpretation.
Rejoicing in that which is accompanied by both vitarka and vicāra, and rejoicing in that which is without vitarka but with vicāra alone, constitute the second.
Rejoicing in that which is without both vitarka and vicāra constitutes the third.
For one who delights in the abandonment of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*)— whether they have not yet attained or have already attained the abiding in happiness in the present life—
it is only after removing the afflictive hindrances that they first attain the four fundamental dhyānas, whether they have not yet attained them or have already attained them.
This is called "dwelling in happiness in the present life.
For one who has not yet attained, or has already attained, the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) involving perception in all their aspects,
there are the lower three empty meditative attainments.
Furthermore, it is only by having severed the lower afflictive obstructions that one attains the various meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) of the formless realm;
as for their basis, these are the four dhyānas.
This is the locus upon which all these merits depend.
For the observer, it consists of the frequent contemplation of the four formless attainments, such as the perception of infinite space, and so forth.
It is for those who take delight in severing the obstacles to meditative concentration.
Regarding those who have not yet attained or have already attained all the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*),
and those who have not yet attained or have already attained all the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*),
this agitation that obstructs meditative concentration is called the "obstruction to concentration" (*samādhy-āvaraṇa*).
It is also called the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
It refers to those practitioners who have reached the ultimate stage of views and inclinations,
whether they have not yet attained or have already attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
One who clings to the perception of compassion as ultimate *nirvāṇa*, and who,
having reached the ultimate vision of the tracks, claims to have attained the final realization through the complete and irrevocable cessation of the six bases of contact (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*).
Having already abandoned the six internal sense bases, one has also permanently severed the six external sense bases.
Twenty-one [qualities] clarify the three virtues of a lay follower (*upāsaka*).
Regarding those who are said to be "wise" in being able to induce both similar and dissimilar dharmas:
Contaminated knowledge is called "conformable to the dharma" (sādharmya),
while uncontaminated knowledge is called "non-conformable to the dharma" (visādharmya). Furthermore, it is explained as follows:
A fellow student who is a lay follower (*upāsaka*) is called one of "identical Dharma" (*sadharmā*).
Others—laypeople who are not fellow students and the five groups of renunciants—are called those of "different Dharma" (*visadharman*).
Twenty-second: the clarification of the three dharmas, beginning with hearing the Dharma.
First, the three dharmas are presented in general;
subsequently, the correct is revealed in contrast to the false.
Furthermore, the teachings of non-Buddhists are erroneous expositions, which is to say, they are false teachings heard.
Regarding the statement that "all prohibitive precepts are not directly perceptible" and so forth:
this is because the ascetic practices and observance of precepts by non-Buddhists have causes but no perceptible fruits;
therefore, they are teachings of false practice.
All meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) that involve affliction and are not ultimate are dharmas of false realization;
the opposite of these is called "correct.
Twenty-three [points] clarify the attainment and relinquishment of defilement and purity.
First, the sequence of attaining and relinquishing the five desires is distinguished;
subsequently, the purity of the Dharma and the definitive tenet that there is no falling back are distinguished.
Regarding the first of these, "attainment" refers to being born in the heavens through the practice of giving and ethical discipline, thereby experiencing the five desires.
Subsequently, one abandons the two types of desire due to their faults;
that is, by means of the virtues of renunciation and seclusion.
Here, "renunciation" refers to abandoning the objects of the five sensory desires, such as forms and so forth, which is called the abandonment of objective desire (*vastukāma*).
Because one is far removed from afflictions, it is called "the desire to abandon afflictions.
Twenty-fourth, clarifying the expulsion of those who violate the precepts due to three conditions,
as in the text.
Twenty-five: It is explained that through four causes and conditions, ethical discipline (*śīla*) gives rise to profound joy.
First, by following the teacher’s instruction to avoid the two extremes of suffering and pleasure;
second, by the attenuation of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Third, obtaining good companionship;
fourth, being free from indolence;
twenty-sixth, clearly understanding the fourfold observation of śīla.
First, one knows through cohabitation that [the precept] exists;
that is, by living together with someone, one comes to know that they possess ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Second, one knows through adversity that it is firm and steadfast.

Regarding "firmness of mind amidst calamities": it means that even while engaged in worldly affairs, one's right faith and right wisdom remain without deficiency or diminution. Regarding "the third, through worldly affairs, knowing with certainty that there is no deficiency":
although one may tread upon worldly duties, one’s correct faith and correct wisdom are entirely free from lack or decline.
Fourth, regarding "resolving through discourse by means of faith and knowledge that is free from attachment and unshakable right view":
this refers to having faith and knowledge that one has no lingering attachment toward any phenomena, whereby one's right view remains unshakable; thus, it fulfills the aforementioned precept.
Twenty-seventh, the explanation of the three types of mental inclinations has two sections.
In the first section, Jing says:
"First, those who weary of clamor and bustle have a mental inclination toward seclusion."
Second, those who weary of wandering through villages and whose minds incline toward renunciation;
and second, those who dwell only in secluded places and possess the perception of tranquility and insight (śamatha-vipaśyanā), whose minds incline toward nirvāṇa.
Regarding the phrase "śamatha, etc.," the term "etc. includes vipaśyanā.
Among these, the first [instance] refers to approaching the forest hermitage (*araṇya*);
the second refers to the mind’s inclination toward renunciation.
Within the second set, the first refers to approaching the forest hermitage for the sake of abandoning the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Second, desiring to transcend birth and death, one leaves the household life and receives the prātimokṣa precepts.
Third, having transcended birth and death, one enters the palace of nirvāṇa; this is called "tending toward nirvāṇa."
The name "nirvāṇa" briefly has five aspects.
The first is that it is the shadow of feeling;
when all feelings are extinguished, it is called "shadowless."
The second is that the continuity is the body;
the extinction of the body is called "nirvāṇa" (quiescence).
The latter three names can be understood according to the text.
Twenty-eight explains that one cannot listen without error due to three faults;
the textual phrasing is easily understood.
Twenty-nine explains that there are five characteristics for being a vessel for hearing and cultivation.
Because it mentions the beginning and encompasses the end, it says "hearing and cultivation" (*śruta-bhāvanā*).
If expressed fully, one should say "the vessel for hearing, reflection, and cultivation" (*śruta-cintā-bhāvanā-bhājana*).

In the *Triṃśikā-vijñapti*, when describing the five qualities of a teacher, the phrase "skillfully establishing the Dharma" refers to skillfully expounding the transformative teachings (*pariyatti-dhamma*).
"Establishing what is to be learned" refers to the establishment of the formal teachings.
Thirty-one explains that the vision of selflessness can lead to liberation.
Thirty-two explains how the four virtues induce the four joys.
This can be understood according to the text.
Third, it clarifies that the Buddha-dharma is called "well-spoken" (svākhyāta).
There are eight pairs of phrases.
The subsequent section explains the preceding.
As for *stūpa*, its translated name is "Exalted and Victorious" (*gāoshèng*);
it is also translated as "Place of Offerings."
For two reasons, physical remains are left behind and a stūpa is established:
first, because that which has been realized abides firmly;
second, because there is a basis upon which to rely.
Thirty-fourth, it clarifies the four kinds of factors that obstruct the abandonment [of defilements].
One should know that regarding those who perform evil deeds, the "eye of wisdom" is said to be blind;
because those who commit evil lack the eye of wisdom, they are called blind.
Those who perform meritorious deeds are said to be "defiled.
Because they lack the eye of wisdom, their performance of merit does not transcend conceptual signs; therefore, it is called "defiled.
Among the various non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), they are said to be "obscured."
Because one lacks the true eye of wisdom, it is said that there is a cataract.
The thirty-fifth [section] explains the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Knowing the eleven defilements refers to the eleven pairs of dharmas in the *Abhidharmakośa*, such as those with greed and those without greed, and so forth.
The "four aggregations and five dispersals" refers to the concise and extensive explanations of the mind in that treatise.
The thirty-six [points] clarify the supramundane path which employs the mundane path as an aid;
by inducing weariness toward decay and ruin, they cause the seeds to wither so that they cannot summon retribution.
37. It is clear that the Tathāgata’s divine eye pervades all objects.
4. He directly perceives sentient beings undergoing death and birth within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). Jing says:
The intermediate state (antarābhava) definitely exists in the realms of desire and form;
however, in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), there is no intermediate state at all.
How then can the divine eye perceive the formless realm?
With the divine eye, the Tathāgata perceives the place where the death-existence (*cyuti-bhava*) of beings in the two lower realms ceases;
he knows that no intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) arises, and that they are reborn in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Tai said: "Even those whose karmic activities are swift and sharp within the realms of desire and form do not have an intermediate state (antarābhava); the Buddha perceives them all."
Furthermore, it is explained that beings in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) have no intermediate state (antarābhava), yet they are also known to undergo death and rebirth along with their retinues.
Thirty-eight [points] clarify the seven gradual stages of realization and penetration into all phenomena.
Regarding the statement that "by exerting diligent effort, one reaches the purification of obstacles":
the Dharma is the internal gift and material wealth is the external gift.
These internal and external gifts are [offered] with an impartial mind.
It is because one cannot provide the skillful means for the arising of the essence of meditative concentration;
through diligence, one abandons these obstacles to the skillful means for the arising of concentration and thereby attains purity.
Thirty-nine [factors] serve as the remedies for the nine types of objects to be remedied by cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

Of these, the first three are the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) as their remedy; the next two are the foundation of mindfulness of feeling (*vedanāsmṛtyupasthāna*) as their remedy.
The next two [types of] minds are eliminated by mindfulness of the mind (*cittānusmṛti*); the final two are eliminated by mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmānusmṛti*).
Forty [points] clarify that there are five faults each for both the ordained and the laity.
Regarding the fault of not delighting [in practice]:
it refers to not taking delight in the precepts one has undertaken to study.
Regarding the fault of associating with those who obstruct the various desires: [it refers to...]
The various desires that obstruct the path are called "obstructors.
There are five further sequences explaining the characteristics of the foolish person.
Regarding the phrase "rejoicing in what is improper": [it refers to...]
This is because one should not give rise to joy in places where it is inappropriate to rejoice.
Regarding the phrase "certainly arduous," it means that the suffering brought about by evil karma is certain and will never fail to occur.
Forty-second: The analogy that birth and death are like the ocean and cannot be drunk.
Just as people on land do not drink the salt water of the worldly ocean, so too the noble ones (ārya) do not drink from the great ocean of birth and death.

Regarding that which is the basis for the great jewel: just as the ocean in the world contains many precious treasures, so too does the great ocean of birth and death contain the great jewel of the Buddha-nature—the naturally existing, untainted seeds.
43. There are five points concerning how the gift of Dharma is superior to the gift of material wealth.
44. One should cause the five types of mind to revolve according to oneself, rather than allowing oneself to revolve according to the mind.
Forty-five: It is explained that various delusive afflictions (*kleśa-mārīcī*) are more severe than demonic spirits.
Forty-six: It is explained that establishing a self involves faults, as detailed in the text. Forty-seven:
The relationship between the remedial factors (*pratipakṣa*) and their objects (*vipakṣa*) is distinguished by means of the three types of practice.
Those who practice sensual desire experience the five objects of desire.
Those who practice meritorious action experience worldly blessings.
Those who practice the practice of dwelling together experience dwelling in detachment.
Based on these three types of conduct, there are six kinds of attachment and aversion, four bases, and five antidotes.
Regarding the first six:
First, greed for objects;
second, increased hatred toward enemies;
third, greed following false teachings.
The fourth is the intensification of hatred toward others' superior happiness, preventing them from obtaining it;
the fifth is the arising of covetous desire for virtuous persons and the withholding of gifts.
Sixth, one gives rise to anger toward those who have faults and is unwilling to bestow gifts upon them.
Because of this, there is an inequality in the mind of aversion;
although one practices the merit of giving, one constantly seeks out the recipient as a field of merit.
Internally, one dwells in a state of ruin, sorrow, suffering, and lack of peace.
Regarding the four bases:
first, the objective sphere serves as the basis.
This refers first to craving for objects.
As for the statement that "other sentient beings serve as the basis," the remaining five types arise with respect to sentient beings.
Furthermore, regarding the fact that each of the first two bases gives rise to a portion of affliction:
in the first, there is only craving toward the object;
in the second, there is only aversion toward the enemy.
Regarding the statement that "the remaining bases each give rise to both partial and total afflictions":
in the third case, one gives rise to greed in accordance with the teachings and subsequently produces other afflictions;
in the fourth case, although one directs anger toward sentient beings who possess superior happiness.
Desiring that others also give rise to greed and so forth themselves;
fifth, giving rise to greed toward those with virtuous qualities,
and subsequently giving rise to other afflictions as well.
Although the sixth [remedy] may give rise to anger toward faults, it may subsequently also give rise to attachment and so forth;
therefore, it is said that the remaining [remedies] arise individually and share common characteristics.
As for the five kinds of remedies: the four [meditations on] impurity and so forth counteract the first four inversions.
The fifth [remedy], the perception of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃjñā*), remedies the fifth and sixth [afflictions].
Furthermore, there is another classification of six types of attachment and aversion with five corresponding remedies:
first, craving for things (*vastu-rāga*).
Second, anger toward two things;
third, giving rise to greed for the three poisons;
fourth, giving rise to anger toward the three roots of goodness.
Fifth, one gives rise to greed regarding the three roots of goodness;
sixth, one gives rise to hatred regarding the three poisons.
As for the five kinds of remedies, both impurity and loving-kindness each counteract the former two.
Among the three types of mental attention (*manasikāra*), the first counteracts the third;
the second counteracts the fourth;
and the third mental attention counteracts both the fifth and the sixth together.
The meaning of the text is clear and can be understood.
Forty-eight [points] clarify the five virtues of one who has left the household life.
First, relying on oneself as a person.
By virtue of going forth, one abandons shared material wealth and relies upon unshared ethical discipline;
as one who was dependent on others and lacked autonomy,
by virtue of going forth, one attains the quality of sovereignty.
Third, those who possess the roots of goodness conducive to liberation that have already matured may,
through renunciation, attain the state of an Arhat if they are free from remaining fetters.
Fourth, those who possess the roots of goodness that have already matured after having renounced the world.
If there are those who, through the cultivation of the abandonment of fetters, attain the fruit of stream-entry, they possess the quality of being exempt from the miserable realms;
these are the five types of persons with immature roots of goodness.
By virtue of renouncing the household life, one manifests liberation from the confinement of domestic life;
subsequently, one will surely bring virtue to maturity.
Section forty-nine elucidates the three types of suffering and the nine aspects [of foulness].

The first three are the characteristic of the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*); the middle three are the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*); and the last three are the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*).
Fifty: Clarifying the Four Limbs of Sentient Beings.
First the heading, second the explanation, and third the conclusion.
Within the explanation, there are four sections.
Each [of these] asks about the resolution of the knots.

Regarding the statement, "One who is constantly swept away and drowned by the other four types of stinginess further gives rise to stinginess regarding the Dharma," this refers to the period at the end of the eon mentioned in the preceding text.

In some places, there are five types of stinginess—stinginess regarding dwellings, stinginess regarding families, stinginess regarding gain, stinginess regarding honor, and stinginess regarding the Dharma—which are not fully present [in all cases].
According to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, there are five types of stinginess:
namely, stinginess regarding dwellings, stinginess regarding families, stinginess regarding giving, stinginess regarding preaching and praising, and stinginess regarding the Dharma.
As for the statement that "the remaining four plus the [dharma-]mātsarya constitute five types of stinginess," this respectfully groups two types of stinginess together as one;
it refers specifically to stinginess regarding the exposition and praise of the *Tattvasiddhi* (Chengshi).

Regarding the statement that "the first wisdom is established based on the continuity of being free from defilement and the thorough penetration of the eightfold noble path," this refers to the wisdom of the noble path in an ordinary person who has abandoned false faith.
This refers to the wholesome states acquired at birth (*upapattipratilambhika-kuśala*).
Taking this as a basis, one cultivates the remaining three types of knowledge; these are the wholesome states of application (*prāyogika-kuśala*).
The conclusion below states:
Regarding how these four branches are divided into eleven each, making them equal and equivalent to the four:
within the first branch, five are opened up;
in the second, there are four.
The latter two each have one,
totaling eleven. However,
the individual eleven and the collective four factors are equal in their essence, with no difference in breadth or narrowness between them.
In the seventy-first fascicle, next, the fifty-first section clarifies the seven meanings and the seven joys.
Regarding the meaning of the "seven branches," Jing states:
first, one who desires skillfulness regarding the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth should investigate their meaning.

Second, there are those who are to be gathered through either the gathering by means of their own nature or the gathering of disciples and others through material goods and the Dharma; this is the meaning of "those to be gathered.
Third, there are evil friends and adverse conditions.
One must avoid it; this is the meaning of "should be avoided.
Fourth is the merit within meditative concentration;
one should intentionally draw it forth, which is the meaning of "should be drawn forth."
Fifth, because one should restrain all evils, it is called the meaning of "that which should be restrained.
Sixth, pure precepts and so forth are called the meaning of "that which should be maintained.
Seventh, the five supernormal powers should arise based on meditative concentration.
Furthermore, the possession of precepts and so forth should rely upon reverence for their arousal; thus, it is termed "the meaning of that which should be aroused. Tái states:
"Among the seven meanings, the first one is the teaching (*dharma*)."
The next two are the dharmas of principle:
right principle should be embraced and wrong principle should be avoided.
The next two are the dharmas of practice.
Wholesome conduct should be cultivated and unwholesome conduct should be restrained.
The next two are the dharmas of the fruit:
one should early on maintain those for self-benefit, and one should fulfill those that are the fruits for the benefit of others.
Now, according to the latter interpretation,
the "seven types of joy" refer to the joy induced by the wisdom that takes the aforementioned seven objects as its cognitive support.
First is the joy induced by hearing.
First, through the wisdom derived from hearing, one generates joy by investigating the meanings that ought to be pursued;
second, through the wisdom derived from reflection, one contemplates what ought to be adopted and what ought to be avoided.
Third is the cultivation of wisdom (bhāvanāmayī-prajñā).
It takes as its object that which leads to the meaningful goal;
it is free from hindrances (nīvaraṇa) in the first, fourth, and fifth [dhyānas].

Subsequently, that which takes as its object the meaning of what is to be excluded—namely, internally abandoning the five hindrances and externally subduing the arguments of others—is collectively termed "excluding evil.
The six recollections take as their objects one's own meritorious qualities and wisdom; this is the meaning of "retaining what is to be upheld."
Seventh, regarding the inferior [dharmas], one should not give rise to contentment; this is the meaning that should be developed based on the conditions.
The fifty-second [section] clarifies five kinds of dharmas.
Zhongjing says:
Those who embrace [the Dharma] embrace both material wealth and the Dharma;
those who enjoy the Dharma enjoy both material wealth and the Dharma as well as the teachings on phenomena;
those who realize the Dharma realize the Dharma of both principle and phenomena.
Tài said: "First is the Dharma of Teaching;
second is the Dharma of Practice."
Three are the dharmas of principle that should be embraced;
the next two are the dharmas of result.
The conditioned fruit is the dharma that is enjoyed;
the unconditioned fruit is the dharma that is realized.
The fifty-third [chapter] clarifies the analogy of the bow and arrow.
This explains the three trainings.
The bow is a metaphor for the virtue of ethical discipline (*śīla*), because it serves as the basis for the arising of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The arrow illustrates the virtue of concentration, because it focuses single-mindedly upon a single object.
Among these, "wisdom as metaphor" refers to wisdom that arises based on meditative concentration by taking an object as its support;
it is called "knowing things according to their objects."
If it is a good arrow, the bow possesses two virtues: first, its nature is firm and solid; this is a metaphor for ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Because external conditions cannot destroy it, it is said that its nature is firm.
The second, "well-executed to completion," is a metaphor for the function of ethical discipline (*śīla*) in its orientation toward reaching enlightenment.
The arrow possessing a single virtue, "well-executed to completion," is a metaphor for the function of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) in its orientation toward reaching enlightenment.
There is no failure along the middle path.
Within hitting the mark, there are three virtues.
First, ultimate skillfulness is a metaphor for the wisdom of one beyond training (*aśaikṣajñāna*).
Second, one who has practiced craftsmanship is a metaphor for the wisdom of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga-jñāna*).
Third, one who is learning craftsmanship from a teacher is a metaphor for the wisdom of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga-jñāna*).
This should be verified against the *Maulī Bhūmi*.
Fifty-fourth, clarifying the distinctions and principles of the Buddha’s teachings.
First, the teaching of long duration refers to the gradual guidance provided by the Hīnayāna teachings.
Second, the uninterrupted teaching refers to the sudden teaching of the Mahāyāna.
This refers, for example, to the teachings spoken at the initial moment of attaining enlightenment in the *Avataṃsaka* and other sutras.
Third, regarding the non-repetitive teaching:
this refers, for example, to the definitive (*nītārtha*) teachings of the *Nirvāṇa*.
Fifty-five: The analogy of the five modes of governance for traversing the path, and the two characteristics of *śīla* (ethical discipline) that enable one to go to the happy realms.
Regarding "traversing the path," it is an analogy for the practitioner traversing *saṃsāra* and reaching *nirvāṇa*.
Regarding the remedy for the glare of heat: the parasol that wards off the glare of heat and distress serves as the remedy.
This is a metaphor for when false wisdom arises, the holy teaching serves as the remedy.
Regarding the second, the remedy for perils: where there are many bandits in dangerous places, weapons and soldiers serve as the remedy.
The hells are likened to many perils, and ethical conduct is the fortress that guards against them.
Regarding the three rivers as something to be crossed: for those who cross the rivers, boats and rafts serve as their reliance;
this is a metaphor for how the surging waters of craving are crossed by means of the boat of *prajñā*.
Fourth, the remedy for exhaustion: for one who is exhausted, a drink serves as the remedy.

This is a metaphor for using meditative concentration (*samādhi*) as the remedy for the parching thirst of distraction. Fifth, the remedy for physical fatigue: for one whose body is weary and fatigued, reclining, riding, massage, and so forth serve as the remedies.
The analogy of the skin refers to the treatment [of afflictions] through joy, heaviness,
and pliancy. Regarding the statement that *śīla* has two characteristics and can lead to the happy realms (*sugati*),
this passage cites the first [characteristic] and speaks only of *śīla*.
It is not said that meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) can produce the signs of rebirth; rather,
because they bring one near to the destination and lead one far toward Bodhi,
it is said that they can produce birth in the happy realms (*sugati*).
First, "embracing ethical discipline" (*śīla*) refers to receiving the full ordination (*upasampadā*) and so forth;
"intact ethical discipline" refers to guarding and maintaining the prohibitive precepts.
Verses fifty-six clarify the acceptance of desire and its transformation and decay.
Regarding the statement "the first is coarse transformation and decay," this refers to death at the end of a single lifetime.
The second, "subtle transformation and decay," refers to death moment by moment.
There are likewise two stages of this transformation and decay.
Regarding "the first is coarse and the second is subtle," this refers again to the meaning of the preceding two [stages] as explained in terms of their respective positions.
The fifty-seventh [verse] states that clear wisdom possesses two virtues.
The virtue of correct practice consists of three phrases:
first, "swiftness," which refers to the rapid turning of the mind and mental factors associated with various forms of knowledge;
second, "certainty," which refers to the elimination of doubt by means of various forms of knowledge.
The third [category], "subtle," refers to those wisdoms that are able to penetrate subtle principles.
Regarding the second, the "virtues of intrinsic nature," there are seven phrases.
The first is "belonging to the stage of meditative concentration" (*samāhitabhūmika*), which serves to distinguish this from the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
1. "Irreversible" distinguishes [this type] from the five faculties and the spiritual lineage (*gotra*). 2.
"Supramundane" distinguishes it from mundane cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanā-prajñā*). 3.
"Having already well-cultivated" distinguishes it from those who are newly practicing the Vehicle (*yāna*).
Fifth, "having no obstructions regarding one's own sphere of activity" indicates that there is no impediment with respect to the object.
Sixth, "surpassing all other roots of goodness of its own kind."
It is superior to all other roots of goodness within one's own vehicle.
Seventh, it is superior to all roots of goodness belonging to other classes;
that is, it is superior to the roots of goodness of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Another interpretation is that untainted wisdom (anāsrava-jñāna) is superior to tainted wisdom (sāsrava-jñāna); thus,
it is called "superior within its own class."
Furthermore, those other contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) that surpass contaminated knowledge are called "superior to others" (*paravijaya*).
Among these fifty-eight [categories], three applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) serve as their antidotes.
Regarding the attachment to companions: attachment to the physical body has vitality as its companion for sustaining life.
Contemplating the impurity of the body serves as an antidote;
likewise, when one views one's wife and concubines— who are objects of attachment—
as pure, this is called "clinging to companions."
Contemplating the impurity of the body is the remedy for the first;
contemplating sensation as suffering is the remedy for those who are attached to gain and offerings;
and contemplating the mind as impermanent and phenomena as selfless are the remedies for those who are attached to future existence.
Fifty-ninth: the explanation of the three phrases beginning with "preparatory application" (*prayoga*). Jing says:
these three phrases are established as the basis.
The two preceding sections have fully explained the text of this sūtra.
The application of the practice (*prayoga*) is the counteractive (*pratipakṣa*) to sensual desire and ignorance;
it is the application by which ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) give rise to this suppression of the afflictions.
Regarding the fact that the established and non-established truths are directly perceived as clear realization (*abhisamaya*):
this clear realization arises in noble ones (*ārya*).
As for the continuity [of the practitioner], it is one who has either already abandoned desire or has not yet abandoned desire.
Generally speaking, the state of being free from desire or not yet free from desire within a single body is termed "continuity" (*saṃtati*);
this applies universally to both ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*).

Furthermore, it is categorized according to the basis (*bhūmi*), the category (*prakāra*), the fact that meditative concentration has not yet been cultivated, or the fact that it has already been cultivated but not yet attained.
This is a further explanation of the continuity [of the path].
Regarding "the obstacle to the purification of the basis," this is a further explanation of the clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
As for "because it is an obstacle to the mental attention (*manasikāra*) and because it is the counteragent to that obstacle":
This is because it is a further explanation of the preceding preparatory practice (*prayoga*).
Tai states: "The preparatory practice is a branch of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*)."
Clear realization (abhisamaya) is the path of seeing (darśanamārga); the continuity [of that realization] is the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).
In the body of one who has attained the first fruit, the continuity has not yet abandoned desire.
"The remaining fruits consist of the continuity of the body that has already abandoned desire;
furthermore, it is based on this [basis] and serves as the antidote to those obstacles"—
this first sixfold [classification] further clarifies the preceding preparatory application (*prayoga*).
The body of the desire realm, which serves as the basis for the preparatory application (prayoga),
is comprised within the nine grades of the desire realm stage,
because meditative concentration has not yet been attained.
Having already studied the methods for cultivating meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one has not yet perfected or attained it;
if one perfects them, one then attains concentration—this reiterates the aforementioned preparatory application (*prayoga*).
The "obstacles to the faculties" (*indriya-āvaraṇa*) are termed "obstacles to the purity of the basis" (*āśraya-viśuddhy-āvaraṇa*).
The afflictions and karma are called the obstacles to the purification of mental attention (*manasikāra*).
The remedies for these [afflictions] through the paths of seeing and cultivation are called the remedies for those obstacles.
Xuanzang says:
"Based upon" means that the body in Jambudvīpa is the basis for the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
"Stage" refers to the stage of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*);
thus, the nine grades of greed and so forth are suppressed by the path of preparation.
It can also serve as an antidote to the nine grades of the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*).
Regarding "because meditative concentration has not yet been cultivated," this means that on the path of preparation, the fundamental concentration (*maula-samādhi*) has not yet been cultivated.
Regarding "having cultivated it but not yet attained it," this means that on the path of preparation, the preparatory concentration (*sāmantaka-samādhi*) has already been cultivated.
Therefore, it is said that [the path] has been cultivated;
yet, because the fundamental concentration (mauladhyāna) has not been attained, it is said that it has not been attained;
and because the preparatory concentration (sāmantaka-dhyāna) has been attained, it is said that it has been attained.
Because the preceding chapters have already explained the preparatory practices (*prayoga*),
the phrase "the obstacles to the purity of the basis" refers to the eight unfavorable conditions (*akṣaṇa*) and so forth, which are termed obstacles to the basis.
This refers to the obstacle of retribution; this is the obstacle to the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*).
This explains the aforementioned clear observation (*abhisamaya*).
As for the phrase "because of the purification of mental attention" (*manasikāra-viśuddhi*):
This is the obstacle of karma, which is itself the obstacle of retribution; this is the obstacle to the path of vision.
This explains the aforementioned clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
As for the phrase "because of the purification of mental attention" (*manasikāra-viśuddhi*):
This refers to the karmic obstruction, which is precisely the obstruction to the cultivation of the path;
this explains the aforementioned continuity.
Regarding "because it is the antidote to those hindrances": this refers to the path that serves as the antidote to those karmic hindrances (*karmāvaraṇa*) and retributive hindrances (*vipākāvaraṇa*).
This is the sixteenth [section], which explains the six clear realizations (*ṣaḍ-abhisamaya*).
First, the preceding summary briefly indicates the six kinds of clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
Regarding the explanation of their names— from the first, the clear realization through reflection (*cintā-abhisamaya*), up to the sixth, the ultimate clear realization (*nisthā-abhisamaya*)—
the phrase "six kinds" refers to the enumeration of their number.
Sixth, "enumeration" (*saṃkhyā*) means "category" (*jāti*).
"Definitive observation" (*niścaya-parīkṣā*) is the meaning of "clear realization" (*abhisamaya*.
According to the *Pañcāśatikā-bhāṣya*, there are fifty-five [points] of explanation.
The latter three are the essence of clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
Contemplation (*cintā*) is the cause of clear realization; thus, it is named according to its own nature and its fruit.
Pure faith (*śraddhā*) is likewise named as a cause of clear realization.
Untainted faith is either co-existent with the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) or co-existent with it; thus,
it is designated by the term "co-existent with the corresponding [realization]."
Furthermore, this "clear realization" (*abhisamaya*) is simultaneous wisdom;
it is named according to its essential nature as being co-existent.
The fourth [chapter] states: "the clear realization of the truths through the wisdom of clear realization."
It is named according to the meaning of its objective referent (ālambana) and its essential nature (svabhāva).
The Truths are the objective referent;
wisdom (jñāna) is the essential nature.
"Manifest realization" (abhisamaya) is the meaning.
Regarding the fifth [type],
it is from the perspective of "meaning," meaning that it is called "realization at the limit" (antya-abhisamaya) because it occurs at the final stage after emerging from true contemplation.
Ultimate clear realization (atyanta-abhisamaya) is named after its stage;
because one approaches this realization at the ultimate stage,
it is necessarily an ultimate clear realization.
Next, the detailed explanation through questions and answers consists of twenty-three sections.
The first distinguishes the common characteristics [of those] who dwell in the stage of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) while contemplating the realization through reflection (*cintā-abhisamaya*).
It first arises at the stage of an ordinary person prior to the path of seeing;
subsequently, it also arises during the path of cultivation as the ultimate clear realization.
One never transgresses in five respects.
One does not go to the houses of butchers, prostitutes, taverns, and the like.
Second, the determination of its essential nature:
the "contemplation through reflection" (*cintā-abhisamaya*) takes the wisdom derived from reflection (*cintā-mayī-prajñā*) within the desire realm as its essence.

The clear realization of faith (*śraddhā-abhisamaya*) has as its essence the mental factor of faith (*śraddhendriya*), which is associated with both outflowing (*sāsrava*) and non-outflowing (*anāsrava*) states, and encompasses the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
The clear realization of ethical discipline (*śīla-abhisamaya*) takes as its nature the sevenfold ethical discipline concomitant with the non-outflowing path (*anāsrava-mārga*).
The clear realization of the knowledge of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*) takes as its essence the non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) of the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*);
the subsequent clear realization (*pṛṣṭhābhisamaya*) takes as its essence the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
Its intrinsic nature is the wisdom that establishes both the established and the non-established truths through repeated conditions;
it is the final clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the path of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-mārga*).
If one relies on the fifty-five [moments], it encompasses both types of wisdom.
In this present text, it takes conventional knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) as its essential nature.
That is to say, one forms the thought: "My births have been exhausted," and so forth.
This defines its substance by way of its specific character.
If based on association and coexistence,
its nature consists of four or five aggregates;
it is either bound by the three knowledges or unbound.
One [mental factor] is bound exclusively to the desire realm: volition (*cetanā*).
One type is partially bound to one or all three realms: faith (*śraddhā*).
This portion of it, along with the other three, these four are unbound (*anāpta*).
That is to say, one portion of this faith, as well as the three realizations consisting of morality and the realization at the conclusion of wisdom—
these four are unconditioned (apratisaṃyukta).
One is both conditioned and unconditioned.

Ultimate clear realization (atyanta-abhisamaya) consists of the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna), which encompass both the mundane and the supramundane.
The mundane is bound; the supramundane is unbound.
These four clarifications depend upon others.
Jingyun Buke said:
"Regarding 'one may or may not obtain the remaining support, while all supports may be obtained':
the contemplative realization (cintā-abhisamaya) relies exclusively on the distracted stage of the desire realm."
It does not rely on the dhyānas or the formless attainments;
rather, it is accepted that the remaining five [supernormal powers] arise from the remaining six dhyānas and three formless attainments.
Furthermore, these supernormal powers may be either contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
It can be understood that it arises throughout the nine stages.
Regarding the statement that it arises throughout the nine stages:
it is easy to understand that within the six dhyāna stages there is the morality associated with the Path (mārga-samvara).
Regarding the three types of empty space, how can there be the "precept associated with the Path" (mārga-sahagata-śīla)?
Because that untainted mental intention (anāsrava-manas-karma) is distantly opposed to and prevents the violation of precepts regarding body and speech within the desire realm,
it is also metaphorically established as "untainted precept."
Since it has already been stated that the fourth and fifth clear realizations (abhisamaya) also pertain to all nine stages,
and furthermore, the subsequent text states that only one clear realization attains the fruit of the nine thorough knowledges (parijñā).
It is further stated:
"Once one attains any one [of the fruits], all four fruits are known.
This indicates that the fourth clear observation (abhisamaya) encompasses both the path of seeing (darśanamārga) and the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).

The fifth, the "Manifestation of the Extremes" (paryantābhisamaya), pertains to both the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) and the middle; its arising is exclusively that of the Path of Vision characterized by signs (lakṣaṇadarśanamārga).
Generally speaking, it consists of the sixteen aspects of contemplation (ṣoḍaśākāra) that arise subsequent to the contemplation of suchness (tathatā).
Because all are termed "partial clear observation" (*prānta-abhisamaya*),
as it is admitted that they can arise within all nine stages.
When arising from the body of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), the six types of clear observation are all termed "ultimate clear observation" (*niṣṭhā-abhisamaya*).
It can be understood that [the insight] penetrates nine stages.
If one does not allow that the fourth and fifth clear realizations (abhisamaya) pertain to all three paths and are restricted solely to the path of seeing (darśanamārga),
then one would have to allow that entry into the path of seeing is also attained within the three intermediate stages (antarabhūmi).
This is because the treatise states that the remaining five types of clear realization (abhisamaya) can all be attained within any of the bases;

Or "harmful application" refers to failing to provide support for those who have been kind.
"Neutral application" refers to...
This means that regarding the latter two types of persons, one should apply superior effort (*adhimātra-prayoga*) in teaching the Dharma;
however, by applying only middling effort, one cannot bring about either benefit or harm.
The following clarifies that those who are of an untrainable nature (*avinīya*) cannot be saved by the Buddhas.
In the "Chapter on Self-Benefit and Benefit for Others" within the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, five kinds of incapacity are treated:
first, incapacity is analyzed;
subsequently, capacity is revealed by way of its opposite.

Regarding the statement in the preceding section, "incapacity for application" up to "engaging in correct means," such a person possesses the teaching of the Dharma for nirvāṇa just like other sentient beings.
Having already cultivated the preliminary practices for the stages (*bhūmi*) for a long time, they are said to have a "matured continuum.
Nevertheless, because they have created obstacles to the vehicle of right practice,
they lack the capacity to engage in right practice within this present life.
Alternatively, this may be based on those of the śrāvaka lineage who have cultivated the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) over many lifetimes and,
in this present life, have practiced and perfected the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Due to encountering adverse conditions, one creates various unwholesome karmas and lacks the capacity to cultivate correct application;
"incapacity for the accomplishment of that fruit" refers to the state up until the point of accomplishing that fruit.
Although this person has no obstacles of evil karma regarding the preparatory practices for cultivating the stages (*bhūmi*), because their cultivation has not yet undergone transformation,
they are unable to accomplish the fruit of entering the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*).
Furthermore, this refers to those of the śrāvaka lineage who, although they lack the obstacle of evil karma during the actual preparatory application,
are nonetheless unable to accomplish the fruit of that noble path because their period of cultivation has not been long.

Regarding the statement "incapacity for the preparatory application and the accomplishment of its fruit" up to "incapacity for both," this refers to when one has not yet long practiced while still on the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*).
One cannot accomplish the noble fruit of the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*).
Furthermore, by creating evil karma, one obstructs the cultivation of correct practice.
Regarding the phrase "incapacity for receiving and benefiting," it refers to the lack of capability to cause others to attain great wealth, freedom from want, and peace and happiness.
The karma of poverty is fixed;
even the Buddhas cannot save one from it.
Chapter Four: Determining the Meaning of Reality.
The Chinese version is divided into two parts.
First, the true meaning is distinguished by means of five matters;
second, it is distinguished by means of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
The preceding section has two parts:
first, a brief presentation of five matters to reveal the true meaning;
second, a formal explanation of these five matters.
The initial statement says:
"If one wishes to thoroughly understand the true meaning,
it refers to the two kinds of reality and the four kinds of reality within the *Maulī Bhūmi*."
The two kinds refer to the nature of things as they are (*yathāvadbhāva*) and the nature of things in their full extent (*yāvadbhāva*).
The four kinds refer to the reality established by worldly consensus (*lokaprasiddha-tattva*) and so forth.
Within the formal explanation, there are two verses.
The initial verse contains ten sections.
The first is the general summary;
the second is the detailed analysis.
The third is the gate of existence and non-existence;
the fourth is the gate of the conventional and the real;
and the fifth is the gate of the distinction between the conventional and the supreme truth of the body.
If it arises as the sixth,
if it differs from the seventh,
its characteristic is the eighth.
The ninth is the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha),
and the tenth is the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha).
The subsequent prose section explains these according to the sequence of their respective categories.
"What are the five matters up to the five right knowledges?
This explains the first section, which provides a general overview.
"What are their characteristics? follows below.
This concludes the second section on the detailed classification.
First, the essence and name are distinguished, followed by an explanation according to the text.
Regarding the explanation of the essence, there are five types of essences established for the initial characteristics.
First, if based on the names and characteristics of entities that possess substantial existence,
then all five dharmas are termed "characteristics" (lakṣaṇa).
Second, if based on the names and characteristics as the locus upon which designations are established, [then only one is so termed].
That is to say, with the exception of True Suchness (tathatā), the remaining four are called "characteristics" (lakṣaṇa).
Because they are contrasted with the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) dharma that is free from characteristics,
these four dharmas are termed "conditioned characteristics."
Furthermore, the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the latter four dharmas are also inexpressible.
However, because they can now be proclaimed according to their general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), those four dharmas are spoken of as "characteristics.
This is because they are expressible by way of their general characteristics in the near term, whereas they are inexpressible by way of their specific characteristics in the ultimate sense.
Third, if one relies on the names and characteristics that serve as the objects of focus for the mind and mental factors within the three realms,
then one takes the first three [categories] to be the "characteristics" (nimitta).
This is because both characteristics and names are all objects of focus for the minds and mental concomitants belonging to the three realms.
The principle of these three dharmas is also the object of the subsequent supramundane knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*);
this determination is made because they constitute the majority.
Fourth, if one refers to the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the objects of contaminated [knowledge], it is called "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*).
That is to say, taking only the grasping of characteristics (*nimitta*) constitutes the two kinds of characteristics;
because the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*) is not grasped, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is excluded.
Fifth, if one refers to those things not subsumed under the four categories of phenomena, they are all termed "characteristics."
This refers to the five sense faculties and the five sense objects in their entirety;

the factors included in the various bases of the *dharmadhātu*— namely, the twenty-one [factors] such as the non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), excluding names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and phonemes (*vyañjana*)— are called the second [aggregate], the aggregate of mental objects (*dharma-skandha*).
The fourth true suchness (tathatā) admits no further advancement or regression;
it is of but one single kind.
The third is conceptual discrimination;
the fifth is correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*). Their occurrence is indeterminate, fluctuating between presence and absence.
If one takes only the mind bound to the three realms as "conceptualization," then within right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*),
it takes both the wisdom that accords with reality (*yathābhūtajñāna*) and the wisdom that accords with the measure of things (*yāvadbhāvajñāna*) as its essence. If,
however, within right knowledge one takes only non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpajñāna*), [then it is defined accordingly].

Thus, within the context of "discrimination" (*vikalpa*), it refers generally to the minds bound to the three realms as well as the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) and the wisdom of things-as-they-are (*yathābhūta-jñāna*).
Next, the names are explained:
"five" (*pañca*) is a numerical designation.
"Phenomenon" (*vastu*) has the meaning of "substance.
It is named by following its numerical category and its essential meaning.
To explain the specific names: that which manifests the essential state is called a "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*).
To designate and summon is called "name" (nāman).
The mind and its mental factors (caitta), together with their objects of thought and deliberation, are termed "discrimination" (vikalpa).
Both of these, when taken in accordance with their meaning, constitute correct knowledge (samyagjñāna).
To turn away from error toward correctness is called discernment;
to decisively sever [delusion] is termed wisdom;
to be free from falsehood is designated as truth.
The term "not different" (ananya) is designated according to its meaning.
As for the names of the established entities, they shall be explained according to the text.
What is meant by "characteristic" (lakṣaṇa)? Briefly stated, it refers to the basis upon which discourse is grounded.
This text explains that the four dharmas constitute the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Regarding the other names derived from within these characteristics,
they refer to the designations (*adhivacana*) applied to those very characteristics.
This is precisely what is called a "designation.
Since all phenomena are nameless, one forcibly applies names to them;
therefore, it is called a designation.
Regarding the statement, "True Suchness (tathatā) refers to that which is manifested by the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya)," etc.:
this is discussed from the perspective of the preeminent, and thus it simply mentions the selflessness of phenomena.
Within the explanation of correct knowledge (samyagjñāna), there are two [types].
First, the chapter opens with a question-and-answer analysis.
Second, it cites scriptural teachings to establish and apply their meaning.
Regarding the statement, "Furthermore, for this reason, those bodhisattvas skillfully cultivate the means regarding the five fields of knowledge (*pañcavidyāsthāna*)," and so forth:
Jingyun: The five fields of knowledge (*pañcavidyāsthāna*) constitute the wisdom of knowing things as they are (*yathāvadbhāva-jñāna*).
This is because when a bodhisattva cultivates the five fields of knowledge, [he realizes this].

One must employ non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) and the wisdom of the two emptinesses (*dvividha-śūnyatā-jñāna*) to be able to penetrate the phenomena of the five sciences (*pañcavidyā-sthāna*).
Therefore, the cultivation of the five sciences is also a supramundane practice of the wisdom of *tathatā*.
Tài said: "Because Bodhisattvas seek all-encompassing wisdom (sarvajñā) and sever the cognitive obstructions (jñeyāvaraṇa),
they extensively study the five sciences (pañcavidyāsthāna)."
When subduing the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) by studying the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*),
one severs the seeds of the cognitive obstructions because one dwells extensively in the all-pervading *tathatā*.
Because they do not seek to sever the obscurations of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*),
they do not dwell extensively in the contemplation of the Four Truths and so forth. Likewise,
the followers of the Two Vehicles do not seek to sever the obscurations to the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Therefore, one does not study the five sciences nor abide in the wisdom that pervades true suchness (*tathatā*).
Beiyun states: "This explains that true suchness pervades all phenomena."

Therefore, one who realizes the meaning of *tathatā* (suchness) thoroughly understands the dharmas of the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*). As for the statement, "What is called mundane and supramundane right knowledge? It refers to that of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and so forth": [This refers to] the mundane right knowledge consisting of the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*), the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñāḥ*), and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharmāḥ*); and the supramundane right knowledge consisting of the three doors of liberation (*trīṇi vimokṣamukhāni*), the eight liberations (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*), the nine successive meditative attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpattayaḥ*), the ten powers (*daśabalāni*), and the four fearlessnesses (*catvāri vaiśāradyāni*). This is what is meant by mundane and supramundane right knowledge. Furthermore, regarding the mundane right knowledge of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, it consists of the knowledge of the four noble truths (*catvāry āryasatyāni*) and the knowledge of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). This is what is meant by the mundane and supramundane right knowledge of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. As for the supramundane right knowledge of the bodhisattvas, it consists of the knowledge of the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā-jñāna*), the knowledge of signlessness (*animitta-jñāna*), the knowledge of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-jñāna*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), the knowledge of non-cessation (*anirodha-jñāna*), the knowledge of non-origination (*ajāti-jñāna*), the knowledge of non-duality (*advaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of non-distinction (*avikalpa-jñāna*), the knowledge of the equality of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-samatā-jñāna*), and the knowledge of the non-differentiation of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-nirviśeṣa-jñāna*). This is what is meant by the supramundane right knowledge of the bodhisattvas. Thus, having realized the meaning of suchness, one thoroughly understands these mundane and supramundane right knowledges. This is what is meant by "thoroughly understanding the dharmas of the five sciences. This concludes the section on the five sciences. Next follows the section on the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*). What are the four reliances? They are: relying on the dharma and not relying on the person; relying on the meaning and not relying on the letter; relying on definitive meaning and not relying on interpretable meaning; and relying on direct knowledge and not relying on discursive cognition. What is meant by "relying on the dharma and not relying on the person"? It means that when hearing the dharma from others, one relies on the dharma and does not rely on the person. Why? Because the dharma is the ultimate refuge, whereas the person is not. Therefore, one relies on the dharma and does not rely on the person. What is meant by "relying on the meaning and not relying on the letter"? It means that when hearing the dharma from others, one relies on the meaning and does not rely on the letter. Why?
