Regarding the statement that "the discrimination of the characteristic of suchness is also thus," it means that defiled cognition relies upon non-dual wisdom; therefore,
it is said to be "also thus."
One interpretation states that the "basis of the Dharma" consists of names,
phrases, and syllables, together with the sounds upon which they depend as its substance;
this is according to one perspective.
If one relies on the various directions, it encompasses both matter and mind;
as for the reliance on meaning, this takes the object of apprehension as its essence.
As for the reliance on sūtras of definitive meaning, this takes the meaning expounded by those sūtras as its essence.
The basis of wisdom (*jñāna*) has right wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) as its essence.
Regarding the three bases of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), it should be understood that wisdom is excluded.
As it is with the discrimination of characteristics, so it is here: because they are tainted (*sāsrava*), wisdom is excluded.
If one relies on other directions to perform buddha-work through discernment,
this is called "reliance on names" and is subsumed under "reliance on dharmas. Furthermore, it is explained as follows:
Discrimination (vikalpa) consists of mental deliberation (manasikāra), which is able to manifest phenomena;
therefore, it is called the "basis of phenomena" (dharmāśraya).
Right knowledge (samyagjñāna) is exclusively the "basis of knowledge" (jñānāśraya).
In accordance with reality, there may be the Buddha’s great wisdom performing buddha-activities and the conceptualization of names; therefore, it is subsumed under the basis of phenomena (*dharma*).
Because it is that which is grasped and because it is what is realized through the teaching, it is the basis for both meaning and scripture.
Now, first of all, regarding the manifestation of the characteristics as being comprised solely by the basis of wisdom (*jñāna-āśraya-saṃgraha*),
there are three pairs of gates concerning the five categories of the material and the immaterial, and so forth.
The chapter states:
The name and suchness are both neither of these two kinds.
Since the name is a provisional existence based on form,
and is not a provisional designation for that which is non-form, it cannot be categorically judged as either form or non-form.
Suchness cannot be described as either form or non-form.
If one relies on the gate of conventional designation (*prajñapti*), suchness is non-form.
This is also the case regarding the gates of being visible or invisible, and being resistant or non-resistant.
This is explained in the same manner as the discussion on the formless realms (ārūpya-dhātu).
In this context, if it is said that the Tathāgata possesses the five untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) and the five objects (viṣaya),
he is endowed with eleven types of form (rūpa).
The *Liang She lun* states:
"Within the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*), the eighteen [elements] constitute the form body (*rūpakāya*),
and the four aggregates (*skandha*) constitute the formation body (*saṃskārakāya*)."
In the svabhāvakāya, form and activity are unapprehendable.
The sambhogakāya is not the svabhāvakāya;
this form of the fruit of buddhahood is subsumed within perfect gnosis (samyagjñāna).
If it is said that the Buddhas have no form-body (rūpakāya),
but rather take great wisdom, great meditative concentration, and great compassion as their essence,
then right gnosis (samyagjñāna) itself is formless.
Therefore, in the detailed analysis of the four applications of mindfulness below,
right knowledge serves as the object for only three applications of mindfulness, excluding the application of mindfulness to the body;
this is stated in reference to the fact that Buddhas do not possess a form-body (*rūpakāya*).
Bei said: "For what reason is it that within birth and death, appearances take conceptual discrimination as their essence,
yet one further establishes the reality of appearances apart from conceptual discrimination?"
The matter of the Buddha-fruit is subsumed within right wisdom;
why is it not established separately as a characteristic?
The explanation says:
Because they falsely imagine that there are characteristics external to the mind,
they establish various systems of characteristics according to their conceptual attachments.
The Buddha, however, realizes the principle of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
Because one does not conceive that there are forms external to the mind,
this is subsumed under right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*).
There is another interpretation as well.
The fruit of Buddhahood is subsumed within the characteristics (lakṣaṇa) such as form (rūpa) and so forth;
however, when the subsequent text states that these characteristics are bound to the three realms (traidhātuka),
it refers only to contaminated (sāsrava) characteristics in contrast to conceptual construction (vikalpa).
In reality, they pertain to the unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*). Regarding the six gates of outflows (*āsrava*) and non-outflows (*anāsrava*),
their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) encompass both types.
Just as the body-faculty, its objects, and so forth of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) are called "outflow-free" (anāsrava) because they are dissociated from latent dispositions (anuśaya),
so too [is this case]. Furthermore, another interpretation states:
Because space (*ākāśa*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) are included within these characteristics,
they pertain to both types [of existence].
As for the second [category], following the case of the contaminated (*sāsrava*), their names and conceptual distinctions (*vikalpa*) exist only as contaminated.
The lower treatise states:
"Regarding the exclusion of the truth of cessation from the categorization of the three truths,
according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, there are three kinds of the truth of the path."
The aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) and so forth are also subsumed under the Truth of the Path.
True Suchness (*tathatā*) serves as the path of antidote;
because it is the object of focus for the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), it is termed "untainted" (*anāsrava*).
It is "outflow-free" (anāsrava) because it is not the meaning of an antidotal wisdom that exhausts the outflows.
Furthermore, another explanation is that its characteristic is the exhaustion of true suchness (tathatā) through non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
The meaning of the characteristics of selective cessation and exhaustion is subsumed under these characteristics.
Within the sevenfold classification of conditioned suffering and the unconditioned gate,
suchness has as its objective referent (ālambana) solely the characteristic of bringing all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) to stillness for the purpose of counteracting them.
Therefore, this is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

However, True Suchness (*tathatā*) is not the wisdom of the antidote; rather, it is the meaning of the characteristic of the quiescence of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). Furthermore, another explanation states:
Tathatā (Suchness) is the characteristic of the quiescence of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); it has the meaning of cessation.
This characteristic of the quiescence of all conditioned phenomena is subsumed under the category of characteristics.
There are three pairs of categories, such as those with conflict (*saraṇa*) and those without conflict (*araṇa*).
An example is the pair of "prior outflows" and "outflow-free," or the nine pairs such as the mundane and supramundane; herein,
True Suchness serves as the path of counteraction.
The object of the wisdom that brings all verbal proliferation (*prapañca*) and worldly discourse to rest is termed the supramundane essence of *tathatā*.

It is not called "supramundane" in the sense of transcending verbal proliferation as an antidote to its opposite; rather, it is so named because it is the object of the wisdom that causes all such proliferation and worldly discourse to subside.
Regarding the ten pairs of internal and external distinctions,
the *Bùquē* (Supplement) states:
"That which is exclusively external is subsumed under the *dharmāyatana* (sphere of mental objects)."
Regarding the discernment of correct wisdom as it penetrates both the internal and external:
the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) is internal because it is subsumed under the sense-base of mind (*mano-āyatana*);
the remaining factors are external because they are subsumed under various bases among the phenomena (*dharma*).
Suchness is not dual because it differs from the other four [aggregates] in being internal while they are external; thus it is said to be non-dual.
According to the principle of dharmalakṣaṇa, suchness is an external phenomenon and is therefore subsumed under the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana).
Regarding the statement that "non-characteristics" (a-lakṣaṇa) refer to the meaning of gradual reduction and ultimate brevity:

this is not the same as the case where material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) within the category of differing characteristics gradually diminish until they reach a single, most subtle and brief state, which is then called "subtle" (*sūkṣma*).
Rather, it is designated as "subtle" solely on the basis of the meaning of being difficult to discern.
The chapter states:
"Discrimination is subsumed under that which arises from conditions;
because it universally takes both internal and external as its objects, it pertains to both types."
The subsequently attained correct wisdom is likewise so.
True Suchness (tathatā) alone has the sense of being subtle and difficult to discern;
it does not share the same meaning as material forms (rūpa), which gradually diminish from coarse to subtle until reaching the ultimate atom (paramāṇu).
Therefore, it encompasses both the coarse and the subtle.

The meaning of "correct wisdom" (*samyag-jñāna*) being subtle and "true thusness" (*tathatā*) being the subtle object is as stated in the *Samyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* regarding their mutual inclusion through near and far relations: [The *Samyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* says:]...
Spatial distance is exemplified by India and China.
Temporal distance is exemplified by the temporal gap between a preceding visual consciousness and a subsequent visual consciousness;
thus, characteristics [of phenomena] are distinguished as near or distant based on their spatial location and time.
Because both types— proximate and remote— are encompassed,

the four objects (*viṣaya*) in India and China are mutually inclusive; thus, there are instances of proximity and remoteness regarding the characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*),
and there are instances of proximity and remoteness regarding time.
Because the three— name, discrimination, and correct knowledge— are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*),
they all pertain to both the near and the distant [time periods].
The two kinds of *tathatā* (suchness), by virtue of being both near and distant, are neither of these two kinds.
Because the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) cannot be described as being near or far.

If one follows the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*, both the present and the unconditioned are said to be "near," because the unconditioned is realized in accordance with that [present] direction; thus, it differs from this text.
Bei said: "The two matters of appearance and name are distinguished as internal or external based on their locus;
because both discrimination and correct wisdom are dharmas belonging to sentient beings."
Furthermore, their internal or external nature is determined based on the object of focus (*ālambana*).
That which is internal is termed an "internal object," while the external body is termed "external."
Question: Why is it not stated that "name" (nāma) is exclusively birth (jāti)?
Answer: [Because] the eleven gates of the appropriated (upātta) and the non-appropriated (anupātta) are omitted.
The twelfth section, the gateway of the homogeneous (sabhāga) and partially homogeneous (tatsabhāga),
is easy to understand.
The thirteenth is the gateway of the six pairs, such as cause and non-cause.
The chapter states:
"Because this section clarifies the causes, conditions, effects, and fruits,
True Suchness (Tathatā) is not a cause, condition, effect, or fruit."
Within this, there are four gates:
first, the gate of whether the essence is a cause or not a cause;
second, the gate of whether the essence is a fruit or not a fruit.
The three fruits are called "having causes" because they can possess causes;
that which is not a fruit is called "not having causes.
The four causes are called "having fruits" because they can produce fruits.
That which is not a cause is called "that which has no fruit.
Regarding the characteristics of retribution and non-retribution, [this refers to] retribution.
The five faculties and their objects are maturation; the rest are not maturation.
Because sound is not a retribution, its name is also not *vipāka*.
Within the analysis, the eighth consciousness and the six retributive consciousnesses are *vipāka*, while the others are not *vipāka*;
therefore, it pertains to both types.
Since correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) is not a maturation (*vipāka*),
the claim by various masters here that the transformation-retribution (*pariṇāma-vipāka*) is untainted (*anāsrava*) is incorrect.
Regarding what constitutes retribution and what does not:
Among the marks (*nimitta*) and conceptualizations (*vikalpa*), those that are wholesome or unwholesome and are with outflows (*sāsrava*) possess retribution;
because those that are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*) lack retribution, they pertain to both types [of non-retribution].
Since names (*nāman*) are indeterminate, they do not possess retribution.
However, although the provisional has no substantial reality, it takes sound as its substance;
speaking in terms of this substance, it can also be said to have retribution.
Therefore, it is not stated that it is definitely not retribution.
Right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) is untainted (*anāsrava*), determinate, and certainly does not possess maturation (*vipāka*).
Regarding this, the masters of this region say that untainted karma is the cause of the transformation of birth and death (*pariṇāma-maraṇa*) and also possesses retribution; however, this is not so.
The untainted (anāsrava) can only serve as a supporting condition for tainted (sāsrava) karma to obtain the retribution of the transformation body (nairmāṇika- or vaipākika-kāya).
Therefore, it is said that untainted karma acts as the cause.
However, because the untainted is not a cause of retribution (vipāka-hetu), it does not itself possess retribution.
Bei asked: "For what reason is True Suchness not an efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*)?
The explanation says:
Based on the above four conditions, one should provide two interpretations.
Regarding the distinction between that which is associated with maturation (*vipāka*) and that which is not:
the discrimination of the *ālayavijñāna* is associated with maturation.
Regarding the discrimination of the six or seven consciousnesses,
there are two interpretations in the West.
One interpretation is as follows:
That which is summoned by good and evil is maturation (*vipāka*);
everything else is not. This is one interpretation.
The six consciousnesses are invariably non-resultant.
There are fourteen pairs of categories, such as "with object" and "without object," and so forth.
Mind and mental factors are termed "with object."
It is called "associated with names," "possessing activity," and "possessing a basis in the faculties.
Therefore, it is an erroneous explanation.
Fifteenth is the gate of the surpassable and the unsurpassable.
The chapter states:
Among the one hundred dharmas, ninety-nine all have a superior,
because the dharma of True Suchness (tathatā) exists.
Therefore, only True Suchness (tathatā) is called "unsurpassed," because no other dharma transcends it.
The term "unconditioned" (asaṃskṛta) serves to distinguish it from the ninety-four conditioned dharmas (saṃskṛtadharma).
The object of pure non-conceptual wisdom is distinct from cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and other such [conditioned] states; it is necessarily unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Regarding the sixteen aspects, there are four concerning the three times and the non-temporal: true thusness (*tathatā*) is not of the three times.
The Supplementer (Bùquè) says:
Previously, based on its similarity to the essential substance (*svabhāva*), it was considered unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
now, by subsuming its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) under the absence [of intrinsic nature], it is exclusively conditioned and thus subsumed within the three periods of time.
Bei said: Regarding the two types of commonality mentioned in the previous section on the "Inclusion of Aggregates," these were explained in terms of both aspects;
since this current point refers only to the aspect of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), there is no contradiction.
Seventeenth is the gate of the three realms' bondage (*traidhātukabandhana*).
Supplementing the deficiency, it says:
"The three types of bondage in the desire and form realms refer to the characteristics, names, and conceptual discrimination (*lakṣaṇa-nāma-vikalpa*)."
The same applies to those bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*):
there too, there are the three—characteristic, name, and conceptualization.
Question: If that is so, one should simply say that these three pertain to all three realms of existence (*dhātubaddha*).
Why are the formless realms (ārūpya) discussed separately?
The explanation states:
the two realms of desire (kāmadhātu) and form (rūpadhātu) have two types of names.
This refers to the names used in verbal expression and the names used in mental reflection.
Because the formless realm possesses only the names used in mental reflection, it is distinguished separately.
As the *Chapters* state:

Question: For what reason, while in the previous analysis of the categories of outflowing (*sāsrava*) and non-outflowing (*anāsrava*), true suchness (*tathatā*) and correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*) were said to be exclusively non-outflowing, is it now explained that correct wisdom—whether bound (*baddha*) or unbound (*abaddha*)—comprises both types?
How can it be that correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*) is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*) yet said to be bound?
Answer: Previously, because correct wisdom was discussed in terms of the two kinds of reality within the concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*), it was exclusively untainted.
Now, since correct wisdom in the scattered mind (*vikṣipta-citta*) on the stages (*bhūmi*) is generally stated to be tainted (*sāsrava*), it is said to be bound accordingly.
Bei said: "This analysis shows that the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) of the Tathāgata is exclusively unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*).
The same applies to the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward."
The meaning of "from the seventh stage and below" is not fixed.
If they arise in a continuous succession following the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), they are called "unbound.
If they do not arise in such a succession, they are bound to the three realms.
Alternatively, it may be that the subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) from the first bhūmi upward is non-bound (*apratisaṃyukta*), whereas that prior to the bhūmis is bound (*pratisaṃyukta*).
Or again, the subsequent knowledge of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) is bound, while the wisdom of a bodhisattva is non-bound.
Or yet again, the subsequent knowledge of those in training (*śaikṣa*) within the two vehicles is termed bound, while the wisdom of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is non-bound.
Regarding the eighteenth section, the classification by way of the three natures:
that which is termed "only indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*) is said to be such based on its coarse characteristics, whereas in reality it also extends to the wholesome (*kuśala*).
Because the names and so forth produced from the fruit of Buddhahood and above the eighth stage are of a virtuous nature,
True Suchness (tathatā) is exclusively virtuous.
It is the ultimate good (paramārtha-kuśala), because it is the object of pure, skillful, non-conceptual wisdom.
It is called "wholesome" (kuśala) because it functions as a cause that encompasses the characteristic of producing desirable fruits.
Nineteenth: The Section on the Objects and Practices of the Threefold Wisdom.
Supplementing the Deficiency, it says:
The meaning of the question is as follows: Of these five factors,
how many are produced by hearing and so forth,
or increased by hearing and so forth?
Alternatively, those things made manifest through hearing and so forth are all termed "established" (*sādhya*).
How many of these serve as the objects of the three types of wisdom?
Regarding the answer that "characteristics and conceptualization are accomplished by the three types of wisdom and are the objects of the three types of wisdom":
characteristics are manifested through the three types of wisdom;
subsequently, the appearance of images is termed "accomplished by the three types of wisdom."
Furthermore, once the meaning of the words has been understood through the three types of mundane wisdom (*sāsrava-prajñā*), conceptual proliferation increases;
this [proliferation] is also accomplished by those same three types of wisdom.
Thus, these three kinds of objects are said to be "accomplished through hearing and reflection" (*śruta-mayī* and *cintā-mayī*).
Because the image-aspect (nimitta-bhāga) arises through hearing and reflection,
it is said that "names" are accomplished through hearing and reflection;
these are the objects of the three types of wisdom.
That suchness is exclusively the object produced by cultivation means that through cultivation it manifests and thus becomes the object of cultivation.
Correct gnosis is that which is produced by cultivation.
Right knowledge arises because of meditative concentration;
it is called "accomplished through cultivation" (bhāvanā-maya) and serves as the object of the three types of wisdom.
Based on the fact that it takes the essential nature (svabhāva) as its objective support, that essential nature is the object of the three types of wisdom.
Jingyun: According to this text, correct wisdom consists solely of cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*).
As stated in the aforementioned treatise:
Regarding those that pertain both to the mundane and the supramundane, whether bound or unbound:

from the seventh ground downward, the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) gives rise to two types of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) through contaminated cultivated wisdom (*sāsrava bhāvanāmayī prajñā*).
As for the aforementioned "subsequently attained" [wisdom], it refers to true suchness and correct wisdom (*tathatā-samyagjñāna*), which are exclusively uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
According to the explanation based on the wisdom of ultimate reality (*pariniṣpanna-jñāna*), the nature of the wisdom that is bound to the realms (*dhātu*) is indeed with outflows (*sāsrava*).
This is because it is associated with the realms due to being accompanied by coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*).
Bei said: "Because the characteristics and the conceptualization mutually penetrate one another,
when the characteristics and the conceptualization thoroughly interpenetrate the three types of wisdom, this constitutes the objective realm of the three types of wisdom."
The two types of wisdom—those arising from hearing and reflection—also give rise to vocal karma;
therefore, based on vocal karma, sounds can possess names and so forth.
This concludes the twenty-third section: the gateway of the meditative object of samādhi.
The Director of the Palace Library (Zhongbuche) said:
"Within the marks, there is subsequently that which is with outflows;
because of emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness, these are the three kinds."
Furthermore, because it is also designated as one of the three objects and is not non-conditioned (*asaṃskṛta*),
it is not the focal object (*ālambana*) of the signless (*animitta*).
Its conceptualization (*vikalpa*) pervades all three types.
These two types of objects are designated by the term "suchness" (tathatā),
yet true suchness itself is not of three kinds;
it is the objective referent of emptiness and signlessness.
Right knowledge (samyag-jñāna) is of three types, and its object is emptiness (śūnyatā).
Within the preceding and following contexts, it may take the Truth of the Path (mārga-satya) as its object and be termed "wishlessness" (apraṇihita),
or it may be described as "signlessness" (animitta), or as "emptiness," and so forth.
Now, in stating that right knowledge has only emptiness as its object of practice,
this is a discussion that cites one specific approach;
if there were no distinctions, it would be the same for the three subsequent repetitions below.
To distinguish their differences:
if, initially, there were no distinction in essence,
they would be collectively termed emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness.
Its essence is broad and encompasses the three types of wisdom,
yet it is exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*).
If it is designated as the "emptiness samādhi" or even the "signless samādhi," [it remains so].
It has as its nature that which is accomplished through cultivation alone;
it is both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). This is said from the perspective of the door of liberation of mind alone.
It is taught that [the three samādhis] have exclusively uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) as their nature.
The Sarvāstivādins maintain that there are only two [types].
If one speaks of the three samādhis, they then encompass both the contaminated and the uncontaminated.
If it is said that the three gates of liberation have as their essence only untainted cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanā-prajñā*), Jing says:
According to this text, the samādhi of emptiness universally takes as its object both the contaminated and the uncontaminated, as well as the conditioned and the unconditioned;
the samādhi of wishlessness does not take the conditioned or the uncontaminated as its object.
Because right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) is not an object of focus for the wishless (*apraṇihita*).
Twenty-one: the gate of the objects associated with the three trainings of ethical discipline, concentration, and wisdom.
Supplement says:
Regarding the statement that "the characteristics consist of higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*) and its attendants (*parivāra*)," within these characteristics,
the sevenfold wholesome [actions] of body and speech constitute the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of ethical discipline; the remaining factors,
such as the preliminary and subsequent stages of application (*prayoga*), constitute the attendants of ethical discipline.
Among these characteristics, the subsequent outflow-tainted mind and wisdom are also the objects of cultivated wisdom;
they are called the objects of the mind and wisdom that accompany the retinue of ethical discipline.
The name [of this precept] does not constitute the essential substance (*śīla-dravya*) of the sevenfold bodily and vocal precepts;
rather, the designation "precept" is merely a conventional imputation (*prajñapti*) applied upon the sound of vocal action within the context of the precepts.
Therefore, this name is an attendant of the precepts and is also an object of mental wisdom.
"Differentiation is both mind and wisdom, and it is also that which is practiced by mind and wisdom; it is an attendant of ethical discipline.
This means that because one upholds ethical discipline through differentiation, it is therefore an attendant of ethical discipline.
Right knowledge is the retinue of ethical discipline because,
through the power of this wisdom, it gives rise simultaneously to the ethical discipline of the path,
such as meditative concentration; therefore, it is its retinue.
The chapter states:
"The characteristic (lakṣaṇa) is the primary substance of the precepts (adhiśīla-samvara), which gives rise to action through the two karmas of body and speech;
the four aggregates (skandha) are its attendants."
The name refers to the retinue of the vocal karma of morality (*śīla*).
Regarding the three categories— such as the twenty-two factors of training (*śaikṣa*) and so forth—
their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and their analytical distinctions (*vibhāga*) apply to all three types of learners (*śaikṣa*).
Bei said: "The three trainings are mutually inclusive,
because the three trainings all encompass the out-flowing (sāsrava)."

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* explains that the wholesome factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) are designated as the faculty of "desiring to know the unknown" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*) and as "those in training" (*śaikṣa*).
However, when these same wholesome states with outflows (*sāsrava*) arise within the person of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), they are designated as "beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*).

However, because the distinction between the learned (*śaikṣa*) and the unlearned (*aśaikṣa*) pertains exclusively to that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*), it was stated previously that both "name" (*nāman*) and "discrimination" (*vikalpa*) are solely with outflows.
This concludes the twenty-third section: the gate of the discrimination of the three types of abandonment.
The chapter states:
"Name is non-obscured neutral; therefore, it is abandoned only through cultivation."
Bei said: "Since all names are with-outflow (*sāsrava*), they are to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
If that is so, how are the names possessed by Arhats to be understood? Most authorities judge [them as follows]."
Twenty-fourth, the section on the objects of the four foundations of mindfulness.
Supplementing the text, it says:
Furthermore, one contemplates the suchness (*tathatā*) of the characteristics of the body.
Regarding the cultivation of the application of mindfulness of dharmas through the condition of disintegration:
the previous application of mindfulness of the body, which takes the physical body as its object,
is now the application of mindfulness of dharmas through the condition of disintegration, insofar as one contemplates the body as being subject to disintegration.
Regarding the statement, "One should know that it is the same for feeling, mind, and dharmas":
one contemplates the suchness (*tathatā*) of feeling and so forth; this is precisely the general contemplation of body, feeling, mind, and dharmas.
All suchnesses possessed by these are called the "dharma-smṛtyupasthāna of the destruction of conditions."
The chapter states:
"Taking true suchness as the object-condition is the application of mindfulness to phenomena that does not destroy the conditions of dharmas.
Furthermore, when one contemplates the characteristics of the body and enters into true suchness,"
The meaning that the ultimate and the conventional are non-different also applies to the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) regarding phenomena as objects of destruction.
The characteristics of the three foundations of mindfulness—feeling, mind, and phenomena—are likewise so.
Regarding the cultivation of the three foundations of mindfulness with right knowledge as their object, excluding the foundation of mindfulness regarding the body:
It is taught that the uncontaminated form and so forth known by the Buddhas are not distinct from consciousness; therefore,
within the context of correct wisdom, the cultivation of the application of mindfulness to the body is not mentioned as its object,
nor is the designation "uncontaminated" mentioned.
Because the mind and mental factors associated with outflows (sāsrava) perceive the existence of a name,
they are said to possess only outflows.
This is because uncontaminated (anāsrava) minds and mental factors do not perceive a name or various forms as existing separately from the mind itself.
Name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*).
The twenty-fifth [section] is the gate of relinquishing the precepts by means of an object.
Supplementing the deficiency, it says:
If correct cognition taking true suchness as its object were to permanently eradicate the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*),
then at the moment when the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) takes true suchness as its object,
the self-verifying-part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) would also be severed because it takes that seeing-part as its object.
The *Yun yuan* states that suchness (*tathatā*) and correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) eternally eradicate the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
The chapter [of the *Yun yuan*] says:
"According to what is taught in the West, correct wisdom reflects back upon itself."
Taking true suchness (tathatā) as its object, correct wisdom (samyag-jñāna) is able to permanently destroy the latent dispositions (anuśaya).
If it were to take only correct wisdom itself as its object, it would not be a contemplation of the signless (animitta),
and thus could not sever the afflictions.
Now, this is explained:
because one enters into suchness through the wisdom that contemplates it,
it is said that true wisdom takes suchness as its object.
It permanently eradicates the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Just as with the previous physical marks, one also cultivates the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) which has the destruction of conditions as its object.
If it is said that "language is like a reflection" and thus refers to the wisdom that takes correct cognition as its object:
When taking True Suchness (tathatā) as an object, one should reflect back upon feeling, mind, and mental factors;
this is the cultivation of the three applications of mindfulness when taking True Suchness as an object,
because it distinguishes emptiness by means of wisdom.
The Sūtra states:
"The emptiness of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-śūnyatā) is called wisdom.
This is the twenty-sixth entry into the gates of meditative concentration (samādhi-mukha).
Within this, first the objects of entering impure meditative absorptions (*sāsrava-samādhi*) are distinguished;
subsequently, the objects of entering pure meditative absorptions (*anāsrava-samādhi*) are distinguished.
Regarding the former, the *Chung-pu-kuei* (Supplement to the Middle) states:
Taking the three [objects] of the desire realm as conditions constitutes the coarse obstacle of suffering;
taking the three [objects] of the first dhyāna as conditions constitutes the sublime correctness.
By thus subduing the afflictions of the desire realm through cultivation, one attains entry into the first dhyāna.
...up to contemplating the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and the sphere of nothingness, one attains entry into the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception three times.
Bei (備) says: "By means of the attachment to the dharmas of the respective stages through longing and aversion."
Therefore, with the exception of authentic wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*),
if that were the case, then even the fetters (*saṃyojana*) belonging to Arhats and others would also be authentic wisdom;
would they not then arise subsequently as something not loathed by others?
The commentary states:
There are two gates to the mundane knowledge of Arhats and others.
The first is that which is subsumed under discrimination.
The second is that which is subsumed by correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).
This text discusses this for the time being according to the gate of analytical discernment (*vikalpa*).
Next, in distinguishing the entry into the object of untainted meditative absorption (*anāsrava-samādhi*), one first explains the entry with reference to the seven dhyānas.
Why is correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) not mentioned?
Because the mind is able to enter what is to be entered, it is omitted for brevity.
Later, it will be explained that there is no supramundane concentration at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), and so forth.
Regarding the twenty-seven categories of faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment,
and so forth, Bukei states:
"In principle, faith and the others also take conceptualization as their object."
Furthermore, these will be analyzed as having faith and so forth as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
This is why it is not stated that they are "analyzed by taking those [objects] as conditions.
The chapter analyzes the five faculties (*indriya*) and the five powers (*bala*), up to and including calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), by means of five matters.
According to the *Madhyāntavibhāga*, the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) are situated in the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*) and Peak (*mūrdhan*),
while the five powers (*pañcabala*) are situated in Patience (*kṣānti*) and the First Dharma (*agradharma*).
Because they all exist prior to the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), they are classified as belonging to the nature of the worldly path.
In the stages of *uṣmagata* and *mūrdhan*, one performs the four types of investigation (*vitarka*) and analysis (*vicāra*) by taking names as conditions and signs as conditions;

these are called the five faculties (*pañcendriya*). Thus, names and signs serve as the objects of focus (*ālambana*), while the true suchness (*tathatā*) and correct gnosis (*samyagjñāna*) of the first stage and above serve as the dominant influence (*adhipati*).
Thus they receive the name of the five faculties (*pañcendriya*).
The same applies to the five powers (*pañcabala*).
They are distinguished as being of the nature of self-nature (*svabhāva*).
Taking names and signs as the object of focus,
one practices the four kinds of knowledge in accordance with reality while abiding in the stage of patience and the first [supramundane] position.
In anticipation of the initial *tathatā* (suchness) and correct cognition (*samyag-jñāna*), they receive the designation "powers" (*bala*).
This is just as the faculties (*indriya*) and powers prior to the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) are designated.

Furthermore, the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) prior to the path of seeing are called "factors of enlightenment" because they can attain the factors of enlightenment for the first stage (*bhūmi*).
This is the worldly factor of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) prior to the [first] stage;
therefore, its intrinsic nature is discrimination.
However, when based on the non-conceptual wisdom (nirvikalpa-jñāna) of the first stage, it is called a factor of enlightenment because it is a constituent of awakening.
This is the supramundane, untainted factor of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga), which has right knowledge as its intrinsic nature and takes suchness as its object.
In relation to the path of vision with its aspects, it functions as the predominant condition for awakening to the established truths.
Furthermore, regarding the eight factors of the path, such as right view:
if they are mundane path-factors belonging to a preceding stage, they should be understood to be distinguished by their own nature as previously described;
if they are supramundane, untainted path-factors, they have right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) as their own nature.
The three branches of the precepts are excluded because they lack an object of focus.
The remaining five branches take as their objects both the established truths and the unestablished suchness.
This is because the eightfold noble path emerges from the contemplation of suchness during the stage of cultivation.
One attains the establishment of the four truths as objects;
on the path of seeing, one cultivates the seven factors of enlightenment.
Because one contemplates only suchness, these factors take suchness alone as their object.
Regarding the goal of attaining the merit of the exhaustion of all outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) within the state of training,
with dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*) as the predominant factor,
it is like the various factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*), some of which have discernment (*pravicaya*) as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Alternatively, it is established as having right knowledge as its intrinsic nature,
with suchness as its object, and it serves as the predominant condition for the dwelling in happiness in the present life through the exhaustion of the outflows.
The four modes of practice explained in the *Prakaraṇapāda* that exclude the four bases of spiritual power (*ṛddhipāda*) apply equally to both calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).
Among these, the four modes of practice are said to be "slow" when based on dull faculties,
and "swift" when based on sharp faculties.
The four fundamental dhyānas, which constitute dwelling in happiness in the present life,
are said to be happiness when already attained,
and suffering when not yet attained.
Such is the establishment of these distinctions:

if the four bases of spiritual power (*ṛddhipāda*) are established according to their respective capacities to sustain the conventional morality, ultimate concentration, wisdom, and the sublime Dharma.
This means that by upholding the conventional true dharma of higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*),
the first two— non-attachment and non-hatred— are established;
and by upholding the remaining conventional true dharmas of higher mind (*adhicitta*) and higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā*), as well as the ultimate true dharma (*paramārtha-saddharma*).
The latter two—right mindfulness and right concentration—are established.
The *Abhidharma-śāstra*, fascicle ten, states:
"There are four types of those who practice correctly."
That is to say: the practice with difficulty and slow progress,
the practice with difficulty and quick progress,
and the practice with ease and slow progress.
The "pleasant swift progress" (sukha-āśu-pratipad):
the first refers to those of dull faculties who have not yet attained the fundamental dhyānas;
the second refers to those of sharp faculties who have not yet attained the fundamental meditative absorptions (dhyānas).
The third refers to one of dull faculties who has already attained the fundamental dhyānas;
the fourth refers to one of sharp faculties who has already attained the fundamental dhyānas.
As for the four tracks of the Dharma:
This refers to non-attachment, non-hatred, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
Non-attachment and non-hatred can cause the training in higher ethics to be purified,
as they do not involve the transgression of the bases of training through the doors of greed and anger.
Right mindfulness can bring about the purification of the training in higher mind,
because there is no loss of the object of focus.
Right concentration can bring about the purification of the training in higher wisdom.
Because the concentrated mind is capable of thoroughly knowing reality as it is,
there are the twenty-eight doors of the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and the bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
Supplementing the deficiency, it says:

Question: Regarding the statement that the eight liberations are established based on the ability to liberate from two types of bonds—this refers to the intent behind establishing the eight liberations.
Among the five categories [of phenomena], which one serves as their essential nature? This is the first question.
"By means of what object is it taken as an object?"—this constitutes two questions.
"With respect to what object does it function as a predominant condition?"—this constitutes three questions.
In the response:

First, it is clarified that liberation generally has the two types of knowledge— knowledge of things as they are (yathābhūta) and knowledge of the full extent of phenomena (yāvadbhāva)— as its nature,
because the first seven liberations are the subsequently attained wisdom (pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna).
Master Ji and others state:
Among the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*), the first three rely on five stages—namely, the four dhyānas and the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The latter five liberations pertain to nine stages.
The first and second liberations involve the manifest colors of blue, yellow, red, and white.
Thereafter, one contemplates the suchness (*tathatā*) of these manifest colors.
Therefore, [the nature of these contemplations] generally consists of both types of wisdom.
This passage states that the first two are not exclusively the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
In the third pure liberation (*śubha-vimokṣa*), one contemplates both pure and impure forms.
These exist in mutual dependence: it is in dependence upon the impure that the pure form is obtained, and it is in dependence upon the pure that the impure form can exist.
Therefore, the natures of the pure and the impure are not fixed.
Having understood that they exist in mutual dependence,
one next contemplates their concomitance, wherein there is only pure matter.
There is the following of impure form;
with the presence of impure form, there is the following of pure [form].
Having thus understood the following of characteristics, one attains mastery over the mind through contemplation.
Therefore, the third [stage] consists of observing the single flavor as the mark of purity.
Based on this practice of contemplation,
it is said that one "subsumes the marks within all forms" and "contemplates the suchness of those pure forms."
Respectively, each of the four formless liberations takes as its object the four aggregates of its own level and their suchness (*tathatā*);
the liberation of cessation has no object.
Furthermore, the practitioner below further clarifies the intent of cultivating these liberations.
The first three liberations remove the obstacle of lack of mastery over form;
the subsequent liberations remove the obstacle of lack of mastery over the formless and its cessation.
Next, the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) are explained.
The first four are like the first two [liberations], and the latter four are like the third,
because the first three liberations are expanded to form the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
Since the bases of mastery take form as their object, they likewise possess both types [of objects].
The second is as explained previously regarding the three liberations (*vimokṣa*).
Since beginningless time, one has grasped the pure marks of form;
being led by these objects, the objects prevail over the mind, and the mind lacks sovereignty.
At present, one contemplates form as impure or at times as pure;
one attains mastery over its transformation and relinquishment.
When one is able to prevail over the objective sphere of form, one likewise attains mastery over the four formless aggregates.
Therefore, the superior stages of the contemplation of the mind (*citta-abhibhvāyatana*) are not explained further here.
This is because those who contemplate both form and mind do not wish to distinguish specific superior virtues, as they focus on the boundless.
Although ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) may perform the contemplation of the eight superior stages, they take only form as their object and do not contemplate *tathatā*.
Now, when the noble ones contemplate form and suchness, it is called the "superior knowledge and vision" (viśeṣajñānadarśana).
Ordinary beings, however, are called "those with superior stations" (abhibhvāyatana) merely by virtue of the three general categories;
they do not possess superiority because they take suchness as their object.
The Noble One is further superior because he takes suchness as his object;
this explains the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
They proceed from the four spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*)—blue, yellow, red, and white.
It is transformed into the four colors—blue, yellow, red, and white—and one performs the contemplation of them as pervading everywhere;
therefore, it is said that this is due to the power of the object of focus in the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
It is not merely a matter of contemplating those four colors as pervading.
Furthermore, it is because one contemplates the four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—which act as creators, as well as the suchness (tathatā) of these four material forms.
Regarding the distinctions within this context:

both that which takes the characteristics of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) as its object and that which takes the characteristics of their suchness as its object are referred to by the term "characteristics" (*nimitta*).
According to the first characteristic among the five dharmas, form (*rūpa*) and suchness (*tathatā*) constitute the objective referent (*ālambana-nimitta*).
Furthermore, one contemplates the characteristic of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) and its suchness.
If one does not take as an object that pervasive境 (object) of suchness which is the object of the emptiness-consciousness,
the emptiness-consciousness that depends upon it cannot be established as pervasive.
It is by virtue of the pervasiveness of its object, suchness, that it receives the name "pervasive."
Regarding the statement that "by means of the power of pervasion from the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*),

all liberations (*vimokṣa*) also attain purification," this text explains that the spheres of mastery constitute the first [category], the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) the second, and the liberations the last.
In his commentary on the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, Dharma Master Tai clarifies that the merit of the three categories [of the *dharmaskandha*] is most evident; however, he raises an objection, stating:
"The *kṛtsnāyatana*s (bases of totality) consist exclusively of causes that are invariably *sāsrava* (with outflows)."
Liberation (*vimokṣa*) is exclusively a fruit and is invariably untainted (*anāsrava*).
As for the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), their meaning applies to both cause and fruit;
however, within the analysis of the spheres of mastery, that which is ultimate is designated by the name "fruit."
However, the untainted (anāsrava) encompasses both cause and fruit.
Regarding that which is untainted yet not ultimate:
once the eight bases of mastery (aṣṭāv abhibhvāyatanāni) have attained the contemplation of emptiness (śūnyatā-vipaśyanā), it is termed "untainted."
The eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*) are causes rather than fruits, and thus are not ultimate.
Regarding that which is ultimate but not untainted (*anāsrava*):
when the first of the eight bases of mastery (*aṣṭābhibhv-āyatana*) is initially cultivated and arises, it is the fruit of those [liberations] and is therefore called "ultimate."
Not yet having attained the contemplation of emptiness is called "without outflows" (anāsrava).

Regarding the phrase "this is untainted but not ultimate," this is the interpretation according to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*; however, upon collating the Sanskrit original of the commentary, this passage does not exist there.
There are two sequences for the cultivation of the three categories of phenomena (*triskandha-dharma*).
First, regarding the sequence for beginners:
first one attains liberation, and subsequently one attains the spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana).
Subsequently, one attains the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*). Following the sequence of the two types of emptiness contemplation (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*),
the spheres of totality follow the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and the liberations (*vimokṣa*).
Now, the intent of this passage is based on the subsequent [section] for its exposition.
If that is so, why are the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) explained first here,
followed by the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) and liberation (*vimokṣa*)?
The commentary states:
This refers to the sequence of the teaching, not the sequence of meditative practice (*yogācāra*).
